title: Effects of the Cold War and the Spread of Communism
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: During the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962, American spy planes photographed Soviet nuclear missiles being installed in Cuba, ninety miles from Florida. After a tense thirteen-day standoff and a U.S. naval blockade, the Soviets withdrew the missiles in exchange for an American pledge not to invade Cuba. It was the closest the world has ever come to nuclear war.

The central paradox of the Cold War: the superpowers had enough nuclear weapons to destroy each other many times over, which is precisely why they could never afford to fight each other directly. The rivalry instead spilled out through an arms race, a space race, propaganda, and proxy wars.

In China, a civil war between the Nationalist government and Mao Zedong's Communists resumed after WWII, and in 1949 the Communists won. Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China, bringing the world's most populous nation into the communist camp and roughly doubling the population under communism.

The domino theory held that if one country in a region fell to communism, its neighbors would topple one after another like a row of dominoes. It made even small, distant countries seem vital to U.S. containment policy and helped justify intervention in places like Vietnam.

Mao's Great Leap Forward (1958–1962) was a forced crash program of collectivization and industrialization that produced one of the deadliest famines in history, killing tens of millions of people in China.

Mao's Cultural Revolution (1966–1976) unleashed chaos and violence in the name of purifying the revolution, persecuting intellectuals, officials, and ordinary citizens and deeply disrupting Chinese society.

China's communism was distinct from the Soviet model and eventually broke with the USSR in the Sino-Soviet split. This reminds us that 'communism' was never a single monolithic bloc; communist states pursued their own interests and rivalries.

In Cuba, Fidel Castro's 1959 revolution produced a communist state allied with the Soviet Union right on the doorstep of the United States, setting the stage for the Cuban Missile Crisis and decades of U.S.-Cuban hostility.

Communism often spread because it offered the colonized and the poor a powerful message: liberation from imperialism, landlords, and inequality. Understanding why communism appealed, not just where it spread, links the Cold War back to the revolutions and inequalities of the industrial and imperial eras.

A proxy war is a conflict in which the superpowers supported opposing local sides with money, weapons, advisers, and sometimes troops, while avoiding direct combat with each other. Proxy wars, mostly in the decolonizing world, were where the Cold War turned hot and bloody.

The Korean War (1950–53) was the first major proxy hot war: communist North Korea, backed by the USSR and China, invaded U.S.-backed South Korea. A U.S.-led UN force intervened, China entered on the North's side, and the war ended in stalemate, leaving Korea divided to this day.

In the Vietnam War, the U.S., applying containment and the domino theory, poured hundreds of thousands of troops into supporting South Vietnam against the communist North and the Viet Cong. After heavy casualties and division at home, the U.S. withdrew, and Vietnam was unified under communism in 1975.

The Vietnamese saw their war not as Cold War ideology but as a continuation of their long anti-colonial nationalist struggle for independence and unity, a motivation the domino theory completely missed. The neighboring 'dominoes' notably did not all fall.

In the Soviet-Afghan War (1979–89), the USSR backed Afghan communists against U.S.-backed fighters and became bogged down in a costly, Vietnam-like quagmire that ended in Soviet defeat and withdrawal, contributing to the USSR's later collapse.

The arms race produced tens of thousands of nuclear warheads as the superpowers raced to build ever-more-terrifying arsenals, consuming vast resources and keeping the world under the constant threat of nuclear annihilation.

Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) was the doctrine that because each side could annihilate the other even after being attacked, neither could 'win' a nuclear war. This paradoxically deterred either superpower from starting one.

The Space Race, sparked by the Soviet launch of the satellite Sputnik in 1957 and culminating in the American Moon landing in 1969, was a contest for technological prestige with deep military implications, another arena of indirect Cold War competition.

After the terror of the Cuban Missile Crisis, the superpowers pursued periods of détente — an easing of tensions and arms-control agreements — though the underlying ideological rivalry persisted beneath the surface.

Cold War conflicts were simultaneously superpower proxy battles and local nationalist or revolutionary struggles. Analyzing them requires holding both perspectives: what the superpowers thought they were fighting over, and what local people were actually fighting for.

For the peoples of Asia, Africa, and Latin America, the Cold War was not cold at all but a series of hot wars, coups, and civil conflicts in which millions died. The Korean War alone killed perhaps three million people, and proxy struggles convulsed nations from Guatemala to the Congo to Angola.

The decades of Cold War proxy conflict overlapped exactly with the great wave of decolonization. Newly independent nations, desperate for aid and development, were courted, pressured, armed, and sometimes torn apart by superpowers seeking allies.
